newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Council to try to break deadlock on postal liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: Council to try to break deadlock on postal liberalisation.

text.p: The Irish presidency will try on Friday to get the Telecommunications Council to agree a plan for liberalising postal services in the face of strong opposition to quick action from some member states.
The presidency will try to win ministers over during lunch on a compromise that would set January 1, 2001 as the deadline for opening up direct mail to competition, diplomats said.

Outgoing cross-border mail would be liberalised by January 1, 1999 and the EU would pledge to adopt measures by that date on further liberalisation of the sector, with particular attention to incoming cross-border mail.
But a group of countries including France, Belgium, Portugal and Greece have so far resisted setting an early deadline for liberalising direct mail in the draft directive, COM(95)227.
Any attempt to water down the text, however, would anger countries such as Sweden that favour speedy liberalisation.
The most that can be hoped for is a "wafer-thin" qualified majority on a text, an EU official said.
Some countries might be persuaded to compromise by the threat that the Commission will act unilaterally if the Council does not agree.

The Commission issued a draft notice, 95/C 322/03, in December on how it plans to apply competition rules to the postal sector. It said it would formally adopt the notice if the postal directive had not been agreed by the European Parliament and the Council by the end of 1996.

The notice said the Commission would guarantee that post offices could keep their monopolies over direct mail and incoming cross-border mail until December 31, 2000. A final decision on whether to open up competition in those areas would be taken before June 30, 1998.

The Telecoms Council in June agreed informally several provisions related to "universal service" in the postal sector. They agreed that governments should guarantee door-to-door mail delivery to each person and one collection from each mail box on every working day.

"Universal service" -- the guarantee of affordable service to all citizens -- would include the pickup and distribution of letters weighing up to two kilograms and packages up to 10 kilograms, although member states could raise that to 20 kilograms.
